working_question: Compare MN 2 section 4 pāṇaharānaṃ (painful feelings to be borne) against section 5 caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjeti (avoiding dangerous elephant), using two translations and relevant early context; specify exact verbs and targets, a counter-reading, and limits without inferring a universal safety algorithm.

claims.finding: MN 2 §§2–7 repeat paṭisaṅkhā yoniso; MN 2 §4 endures difficult sensations, §5 avoids dangerous elephants, §6 rejects unwholesome thoughts; MN 4's paṭivinemi addresses fear in wilderness/posture practice. The same external action or shared reflection formula alone cannot determine wisdom; the binary of inner endurance versus external avoidance is an overgeneralization.
claims.uncertainty: MN 2 §4 pāṇaharānaṃ versus §5 dangerous elephant needs two-translation contextual counter-reading; editions and early parallels unresolved.

claims.finding: Observable retreat does not by itself prove inner fear or cowardice. Mil 5.4.9 explains purposeful withdrawal differently from ordinary safety; its story diverges from Vinaya Nālāgiri account.
claims.uncertainty: Not an early discourse definition; original narrative differences and interpretive bridge require independent checking.

claims.finding: MN 4 frames fear-and-posture practice in a specific wilderness training situation and does not supply a universal command to remain physically exposed to threats.
claims.uncertainty: Original Pali verbs and at least two translations of the fear-and-posture passage remain open.

claims.finding: AN 2.9 discusses hiri and ottappa as beneficial guardians; this does not equate ottappa with all fearful states or modern anxiety.
claims.uncertainty: Hiri/ottappa lexical comparisons across Pali editions and early parallels remain open.

claims.finding: MN 61 requires reflection on consequences of actions before, during, and after undertaking them; a modern safety decision framework extrapolating from it is synthesis.
claims.uncertainty: Specific proposed contemporary application remains unreviewed.
